answers.text:
Transfer entropy is a measure of how much knowing a neuron's past activity reduces uncertainty about another neuron's future activity, beyond what that second neuron's own past already tells you. As the article defines it just after this passage, Transfer entropy is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron (e.g., Xp) accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron (e.g., Yt+1), conditioned on Y's own past (Yp). The key phrase is "conditioned on Y's own past" — this is what distinguishes it from simple correlation, since it strips out the part of Y's future that Y's own history already predicts (its autocorrelation), leaving only the genuinely new predictive contribution coming from X.

The reason this measure gets introduced here, right after mutual information, is that it fixes a gap mutual information leaves open. It does not, however, quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure that describes the instantaneous dependency between two variables and has no notion of the time-directed structure that we intuitively understand as "transfer" or "flow." Transfer entropy supplies exactly that missing directionality and timing: Whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity, meaning it captures not just whether two neurons' activity is statistically linked, but whether information seems to actually flow from one to the other over time.

As you may know from outside the article, transfer entropy was formalized by Thomas Schreiber in 2000 as a way to detect directed information flow between time series without assuming a linear model, which is part of why it became popular in neuroscience for inferring "effective" connections from spike trains where the underlying causal wiring isn't directly observable. In this article it plays a load-bearing role later on: it's the tool used to build the "effective networks" from real neural recordings, which are then fed into the partial information decomposition analyses that make up the rest of the paper.

answers.asked: Information-theoretic tools such as mutual information [10] and transfer entropy [11] are well suited to this purpose.
answers.text:
This is pointing ahead to two specific tools the article is about to define, one right after the other. Mutual information measures how much knowing the activity of one neuron reduces uncertainty about another, without regard to timing or direction — it just captures whether two neurons' activity patterns are statistically linked. Transfer entropy adds a time dimension: it measures how much a neuron's past activity helps predict another neuron's future activity, beyond what that second neuron's own past already tells you.

The distinction matters for what "tracking information" means in this article. As the text explains shortly after this sentence, mutual information "can be thought of as a nonlinear correlation between two patterns of activity" and "does not, however, quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure." Transfer entropy, by contrast, is built specifically to capture directional flow: it is "well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron... accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron... conditioned on Y's own past." So the sentence is essentially a preview: one tool tells you *that* two neurons are related, the other tells you *which one is influencing which, over time* — and the numbered citations [10] and [11] point to the original papers that introduced these two measures, which the article defines formally in the next few paragraphs.

answers.asked: What does "transfer entropy" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
Transfer entropy is defined in the article as a measure of how much the past activity of one neuron (X) reduces uncertainty about the future activity of another neuron (Y), over and above what Y's own past already tells you about itself [spya-p4pyuy]. The article gives the formal equation and glosses it as quantifying how much the source's past history "reduces our uncertainty about the future of the target variable, after accounting for information disclosed by the target variable's own past (autocorrelation)" [spya-p4pyuy]. It contrasts this with mutual information, which is undirected and only captures instantaneous shared dependence, calling transfer entropy a measure of "effective connectivity" (actual information propagation) as opposed to mutual information's "functional connectivity" [spya-f6sbgx spya-p4pyuy].

Why it matters to the argument: transfer entropy is the tool the authors use to build the directed, weighted "effective networks" between neurons that everything else in the piece depends on — it is how they identify which neurons send information to which, and how strongly, before ever applying partial information decomposition (PID) [spya-sw5ukx]. It also supplies one of the key correlates of synergy: the amount of synergistic information in a triad tracked closely with the transfer entropy between the source neurons and the target, at about a quarter of its value across recordings [spya-kqkb58]. But the article also flags transfer entropy as a limitation: because the networks in most of the reviewed studies were built from *bivariate* transfer entropy, and bivariate analyses are known to overestimate the significance of edges, this is called out as a caveat on the empirical findings [spya-j4cy9j].

In this abstract, "synergistic" describes one of three ways that neurons or groups of neurons can share information, as revealed by the partial information decomposition (PID) framework the paper introduces. The article defines it later in more technical terms, but the core idea is that synergistic information is information about a target neuron that can only be learned by observing the joint states of two (or more) source neurons together — it is not present in either source neuron's activity on its own, only in the pattern formed by combining them.

The abstract flags this as the mode the authors care about most, describing it as the "higher-order" information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source. The reasoning behind singling it out is that synergy is treated as a signature of genuine computation: a target neuron that shows synergy isn't just adding up its inputs, it's responding to the specific combination of what its inputs are doing, which is closer to what people mean by neural "information processing" rather than simple information relay. The abstract goes on to preview the paper's main empirical finding, that synergistic dynamics are ubiquitous in neural circuitry and show reliable structure–function relationships, emerging disproportionately in neuronal rich clubs, downstream of recurrent connectivity, and in the convergence of correlated activity, which is the pattern the later sections of the paper go on to unpack in detail.

answers.asked: PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources.
answers.text:
This is the abstract's compact preview of the paper's central framework, and each of the three terms names a distinct way information can be shared among neurons—these get spelled out properly later in the article.

The setup, explained in detail further down, is: two or more "source" neurons feed into a single "target" neuron, and you want to know how much the target's future activity is explained by the sources' past activity. Partial information decomposition (PID) splits that total explained information into non-overlapping pieces. As the article defines them: Red(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that could be learned by observing X₁ or X₂, Unq(Xᵢ;Y) is the information about Y that could only be learned by observing Xᵢ, and Syn(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that can only be learned by observing the joint states of X₁ and X₂ together.

In plainer terms: redundant information is what either source neuron alone would already tell you (they overlap); unique information is what only one particular source contributes, not available from the other; synergistic information is what only shows up when you look at both sources' patterns *together*, and can't be predicted from either one in isolation. The paper singles out synergy as the most interesting of the three, since the "higher-order" information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs...is not reducible to input from any single source — this is treated as the closest information-theoretic signature of genuine neural "computation," as opposed to a neuron simply passing along or duplicating what its inputs already carried.

answers.asked: What does "synergistic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
"Synergistic" information is the piece of the joint mutual information that two (or more) source neurons provide about a target's future state which cannot be learned from either source alone — it only shows up when their joint states are considered together [spya-h5jzvm spya-e94ury]. It is formally the term left over once redundant information (learnable from either source) and unique information (learnable only from one particular source) are subtracted from the total joint mutual information, as laid out in the partial information decomposition [spya-h5jzvm].

Why it matters to the argument: the whole piece treats synergy as the signature of genuine "computation" or "information processing," as opposed to a neuron simply summing its inputs. The article states that when the joint information exceeds the sum of the parts, the target neuron performs "a kind of integrating 'computation'" on its inputs — this is what synergy captures [spya-e94ury]. The authors then use synergy as their empirical handle on processing throughout the review: it is found concentrated in rich clubs, downstream of recurrent connectivity, and shaped by how correlated converging inputs are [spya-fud8q3 spya-sd9fzd spya-hkhpex]. In the summary, they say directly that the existence of synergy shows neurons are not just summing inputs and firing at threshold, but are sensitive to the specific patterns of incoming activity [spya-rc5z33]. So synergy is the conceptual pivot that lets the authors move from "information is present" (mutual information, transfer entropy) to "information is being processed/transformed" — the central question the review sets out to address [spya-s0db2g].
